# Climate change drove the deep-time assembly of biodiversity

### Paleoatmospheric temperature data

All climate rasters were aligned to a common spatial grid so that each pixel represents the same geographic location through time. Grid cells were retained only when at least one valid observation was present, ensuring that analyses relied on empirical information rather than interpolation alone. For each grid cell, temperature values through time were treated as a time series, and a smooth trajectory was estimated using a generalized additive model (GAM). Spatially explicit reconstructions of mean annual surface temperature across the Northern Hemisphere from 23 to 2 Ma are shown at 1-Myr intervals and 1° × 1° spatial resolution. Each panel represents a single time slice and is displayed using a common color scale to allow comparison across time. These layers form the basis for estimating directional temperature change and climatic instability used in subsequent analyses.

![**Figure S1: Spatiotemporal reconstruction of near-surface air temperature across the Neogene in North America and Europe.** Panels show paleoclimatic reconstructions of mean atmospheric temperature (°C) from 23 to 2 Ma at \~1 Myr intervals, based on interpolated and smoothed climate surfaces (Hagen et al. 2019) projected onto paleogeographic configurations. Each row represents a successive time slice (Ma), illustrating the progressive evolution of temperature patterns through deep time. Color gradients range from cooler conditions (blue) to warmer conditions (red).](images/clipboard-3710998148.png)

### Obtaining the rate of climate change

Once smoothed trajectories are obtained, temperature change is quantified as the difference between consecutive time steps. These first differences approximate the rate and direction of temperature change through time, allowing spatially explicit assessment of climatic dynamics rather than static climate conditions.

![**Figure S2: Spatiotemporal reconstruction of near-surface air temperature change across the Neogene in North America and Europe.** Panels show paleoclimatic reconstructions of mean atmospheric temperature change (°C/Ma) from 23 to 2 Ma at \~1 Myr intervals, based on interpolated and smoothed climate surfaces (Hagen et al. 2019) projected onto paleogeographic configurations. Each row represents a successive time slice (Ma), illustrating the progressive evolution of temperature change patterns through deep time. Color gradients range from cooling trends (blue) to warming trends (red).](images/clipboard-4291690922.png)

### Estimating climate instability

Climate instability is measured as the standard deviation of mean temperature between consecutive time steps within a moving window of +-2Ma. This captures how variable the atmospheric temperature rather than the warming or the cooling trend. Lower values indicate more stable environments

![**Figure S3: Spatial patterns of paleoatmospheric temperature instability across the Neogene in North America and Europe..** Maps show reconstructed paleoatmospheric temperature instability (°C Ma⁻¹) across North America (left panel) and Europe (right panel) from 22 Ma to 2 Ma. Each map represents a 1-Ma time slice, illustrating the spatial distribution of temperature variability across the continents. Warmer colors (yellow–red) indicate higher rates of temperature instability, whereas cooler colors (blue) indicate lower instability. ](images/clipboard-3915710011.png)

## Statistical analyses

#### Spatial binning of fossil locations into fossil paleoassemblages

Fossil occurrences were aggregated into standardized paleoassemblages using a spatiotemporal binning procedure. Records were first assigned to continents and then spatially grouped into regularly spaced bins (\~100 km) to reduce the effects of uneven sampling intensity. Each spatial bin was combined with a discrete temporal bin based on rounded midpoint ages to define unique spatiotemporal assemblages. These paleoassemblages provide comparable units of community composition for subsequent analyses of turnover and paleobiogeographic structure.

![**Figure S4: Paleocoordinates were used to assign fossil occurrences to a discrete grid of hexagonal cells of approximately 100 × 100 km in geographic space**. Fossil occurrences falling within the same grid cell and Neogene stage were grouped into a single paleoassemblage, which served as the fundamental unit for subsequent diversity, compositional, and network analyses.](images/clipboard-320948014.png)

#### Temporal binning of fossil locations into fossil paleoassemblages

![**Figure S5: Temporal distribution of fossil localities across the Neogene.** Bars show the log-transformed number of fossil localities per 1-Myr time bin, plotted against geological time (Ma). The reversed x-axis follows geological convention, with older ages on the left and younger ages on the right, illustrating changes in sampling intensity through time.](images/clipboard-865054988.png)

#### Estimating turnover among fossil paleoassemblages

We estimated compositional turnover among paleoassemblages using genus-level presence–absence data. It first converts the fossil occurrences into a *genus* × *paleoassemblage* incidence matrix, then removes poorly sampled paleoassemblages by requiring a minimum number of observations (`default: >3`). Abundances are reduced to presence–absence to focus on composition rather than counts. Pairwise dissimilarities are then computed among paleoassemblages using the Simpson-based turnover component (`β_SIM`) from the *betapart* framework, yielding a matrix that quantifies the degree of taxonomic replacement (turnover) between all pairs of paleoassemblages.

![**Figure S6: Pairwise compositional dissimilarity across space and time.** Heatmaps show pairwise Simpson dissimilarity (β_SIM) among fossil paleoassemblages for all taxa, herbivores, and carnivores. Colors represent increasing compositional dissimilarity from low (dark) to high (yellow), highlighting differences in turnover structure among trophic groups across spatiotemporal assemblages.](images/clipboard-1792363359.png)

#### Sensitivity analyses

We tested four model configurations that represent different assumptions about how smooth temperature trajectories are through time. When analyzed together, they provide a sensitivity analysis to understand the impact of different temporal smoothing choices for the shape of temporal climatic trajectories and climate-fossil turnover relationships.

#### Sensitivity of Neogene temperature‐change estimates

-   **gam_6_3 (df = 6, degree = 3):** Allows relatively high flexibility. Temperature trajectories can follow finer temporal variation while remaining smooth, capturing long-term trends as well as moderate shorter-term fluctuations.

-   **gam_4_3 (df = 4, degree = 3):** An intermediate level of smoothing. With fewer degrees of freedom, the model emphasizes broader temporal patterns while still allowing nonlinear trajectories.

-   **gam_4_2 (df = 4, degree = 2):** A more conservative specification. Lower polynomial degree and fewer degrees of freedom produce smoother trajectories that highlight long-term climatic change while reducing sensitivity to short-term variation.

-   **gam_8_3 (df = 8, degree = 3):** The most flexible specification. With more degrees of freedom, the model can track finer-scale temporal changes, allowing the fitted trajectory to follow more detailed fluctuations in the temperature reconstructions.

![**Figure S10: Smoothed trajectories of mean atmospheric temperature across the Neogene under alternative GAM specifications.** Mean atmospheric temperature (°C) from 23 to 2 Ma is shown as smoothed trajectories estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with different smoothing parameters (df = 6, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 2; df = 8, degree = 3). Time is shown in millions of years ago (Ma), with older ages to the left. Lines illustrate how alternative smoothing assumptions affect the reconstructed temporal trajectory of temperature used in subsequent analyses.](images/clipboard-2759316063.png)

![**Figure S11: Estimated rates of temperature change across the Neogene under alternative GAM specifications.** Mean rates of atmospheric temperature change (°C Myr⁻¹) from 23 to 2 Ma are shown for trajectories estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with different smoothing parameters (df = 6, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 2; df = 8, degree = 3). Time is shown in millions of years ago (Ma), with older ages to the left. Lines illustrate how different smoothing assumptions influence the estimated temporal pattern of temperature change used in subsequent analyses.](images/clipboard-515109549.png)

Temperature instability (°C Myr⁻¹), calculated as the absolute rate of temperature change, is shown from 23 to 2 Ma using trajectories derived from generalized additive models (GAMs) with different smoothing parameters (df = 6, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 3; df = 4, degree = 2; df = 8, degree = 3).
